# The Mae Hong Son Loop

> 600 kilometres, 1,864 curves on the sign, and a different answer from the map

A bilingual (English and Thai) directory and route guide for the Mae Hong Son loop in northern Thailand, built from 115 named sources. Every claim carries a provenance tier. Records are CC BY 4.0.

## What is measured here, and how

- Curve counts are computed from OpenStreetMap way geometry: ways carrying each route number are stitched, resampled every 60 m, and walked accumulating heading change; an arc over 25 degrees is a curve, over 120 a hairpin. Route 1095 measures 184.9 km and 1056 curves, 110 of them hairpins. This measures a volunteer trace, not a road survey.
- The roadside sign and merchandise carry 1,864 for the Chiang Mai–Pai road; Thai Wikipedia's Route 1095 article says 'more than 2,000'. Over the Mae Malai–Pai span this project counts 395 at a 25-degree threshold. All three figures are printed with their methods.
- Route 1096 (Samoeng) measures the densest curves on this network at 4.46/km, ahead of Route 1095 at 4.03.
- Air: 15,050 point-days of modelled daily PM2.5 at ten points, Aug 2022 onward, from Copernicus CAMS via Open-Meteo. The model never exceeded 99.4 µg/m³ daily mean; ground stations have recorded far higher.
- Mae Hong Son province (12,765 km²) has 1 official PM2.5 monitor. Pai, Soppong, Khun Yuam and Mae Sariang have none.
- 9,319 places harvested from OpenStreetMap inside the corridor.

# Full records

## Chiang Mai to Pai (leg/cnx-to-pai)
Thai: เชียงใหม่ – ปาย

### what
Route 107 north out of the city to the Route 1095 turn, then over the hills to Pai. The shortest leg of the circuit by distance and the one people most often underestimate by time.

### story
The first thirty-five kilometres are Route 107, which is a wide, busy road out of a city and is not what you came for. The ride begins at the turn.

*Inference —* measured off the OSM trace, the Mae Malai to Pai section of Route 1095 is 94.5 kilometres carrying **580 curves** at a 25-degree threshold, 65 of them hairpins — 4.28 curves a kilometre, the densest sustained stretch on the whole circuit. The hardest two kilometres measured anywhere on 1095 are in here, at 7.45 curves a kilometre.

What that means in practice is that the hundred kilometres takes three hours, not ninety minutes, and it takes longer than that if you stop — which you will, because the climb out of the Mae Taeng valley has the views.

This is also the leg the merchandise is about. The sign says 1,864 curves; the count over this span says 395 at 25 degrees, 450 at 15. What 1,864 would mean over 94.5 kilometres is a curve every 51.9 metres.

Provenance: harvested · s:mhs-measured
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:thwp-1095, s:osm

## Hot to Chiang Mai (leg/hot-to-cnx)
Thai: ฮอด – เชียงใหม่

### what
The commute home. Four to six lanes with a median, narrowing to two through the town centres.

### story
88 kilometres, per the Thai highway article, four to six lanes except through the centres of Hang Dong, San Pa Tong, Thung Sieo and Chom Thong where it drops to two.

*Inference —* two things worth saying about a leg that is otherwise just a road. First, it is where tired riders relax and traffic increases at the same time, which is not a good combination — the circuit's easiest riding is at the end of its longest day. Second, Chom Thong is the turn for Doi Inthanon, so a rider with an extra day has a reason to stop here rather than push in.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:thwp-108, s:wp-chom-thong

## Khun Yuam to Mae Sariang (leg/khun-yuam-to-mae-sariang)
Thai: ขุนยวม – แม่สะเรียง

### what
Ninety-odd kilometres of Route 108 that the Thai highway article describes as running parallel to the Yuam river.

### story
The article is precise about what this road does: from Mae Sariang it parallels the Yuam through Mae La Noi, then climbs after Ban Mae La Luang to Khun Yuam. A river road with a climb at the north end.

*Inference —* it is the leg where the trip changes pace. The riding asks little, the villages are frequent, and the temptation is to cover it fast. The villages are exactly why not to: this is Karen country and the roadside is where most of what you will see of it happens.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:thwp-108, s:wp-mae-la-noi-district, s:wp-karen-peoples

## Mae Sariang to Hot (leg/mae-sariang-to-hot)
Thai: แม่สะเรียง – ฮอด

### what
The emptiest stretch of the circuit. Sealed, two lanes, steep hillsides, few villages, and a national park in the middle.

### story
The Thai highway article puts it plainly: from Hot the road runs along steep hills all the way to Mae Sariang. Between the two there is Op Luang, a gorge the Chaem river cut, and not a great deal else with a name.

*Inference —* the planning points are fuel and heat. This is the longest gap between towns of any size on the circuit, it is low and hot at the eastern end, and it is where a day that started late finishes in the dark. Counter-clockwise it is day one and it is a very long day one; clockwise it is the last real leg and it is the one that gets rushed.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:thwp-108, s:wp-op-luang-national-park, s:wp-hot-district

## Mae Hong Son to Khun Yuam (leg/mhs-to-khun-yuam)
Thai: แม่ฮ่องสอน – ขุนยวม

### what
Route 108 south. The climb out of the Mae Hong Son valley, then the first of the long southern running.

### story
The Thai Wikipedia article describes this section from the other end: the road crosses the mountains to drop into Mae Hong Son town, having climbed from Ban Mae La Luang past Khun Yuam. Ridden southbound you do that in reverse — climb out, then run.

*Inference —* the change of character is the thing to expect. After three days of 1095 this feels open and fast, and the curves that remain are longer-radius. Riders who have adjusted to nearly six curves a kilometre take a leg or so to recalibrate, which is its own small hazard.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:thwp-108, s:wp-khun-yuam-district

## Pai to Soppong (leg/pai-to-soppong)
Thai: ปาย – สบป่อง

### what
Short. Out of the Pai basin, up, and into limestone country.

### story
*Inference —* measured off OSM this section carries 139 curves in 36.7 kilometres, 3.87 a kilometre. It is the easiest of the three 1095 sections by that measure, and the shortest by a long way.

Which makes it the leg to use. A day that runs Pai to Soppong only is a half day with the caves in it; a day that runs Pai to Mae Hong Son is a full one that ends with the hardest descent of the northern leg. *Inference —* people who are tired when they reach Mae Hong Son usually made that choice without noticing it was one.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:wp-pang-mapha-district

## The Samoeng warm-up (leg/samoeng-warmup)
Thai: วงรอบสะเมิง ซ้อมใหญ่

### what
Chiang Mai to Mae Rim, Route 1096 to Samoeng, and back. A day. Not part of the loop.

### story
*Inference —* this is the single most useful thing on this site for a rider who is not sure, and it costs a day.

Measured off OSM, Route 1096 carries **6.34 curves a kilometre** over its 29.8-kilometre run — the densest road measured anywhere on this network, against Route 1095's 5.71. So the Samoeng day is the same riding in miniature, an hour from a city with a hospital, on the bike you have just rented, with your luggage still in the room.

What it tells you: whether the rental is sound, whether the brakes fade, whether your wrists last, whether a pillion enjoys it, and whether four days of this is a holiday or an ordeal. Anyone who finishes it tired and happy should go. Anyone who finishes it tired and quiet has learned something worth a day.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:wp-samoeng-district

## Soppong to Mae Hong Son (leg/soppong-to-mhs)
Thai: สบป่อง – แม่ฮ่องสอน

### what
Fifty-two kilometres, a hundred and ninety curves, and a long drop into the Mae Hong Son valley at the end.

### story
*Inference —* 51.5 kilometres, 190 curves at a 25-degree threshold, 3.74 a kilometre. On paper the gentlest of the three 1095 sections; in practice the one with the most sustained descent.

This is the leg the light argument is about. Ridden westward in the afternoon in the cool season the sun sits at the end of the road, on two lanes, with oncoming traffic, for the last hour. Ridden eastward in the morning it is behind you. *Inference —* it is the clearest single reason in the whole clockwise-versus-counter-clockwise question to consider going the other way round, and almost nobody raises it.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:wp-mae-hong-son

## The 1263 cut (leg/the-1263-cut)
Thai: ทางลัด 1263

### what
Khun Yuam east to Mae Chaem. Optional. A three-day loop instead of a four-day one, bought with the steepest and most curve-dense road here.

### story
*Inference —* over the 38.1 kilometres OpenStreetMap has mapped of it: 159 curves at a 25-degree threshold, 25 hairpins, **4.25 a kilometre — denser than Route 1095**, with a fraction of the traffic and none of the infrastructure. The road runs roughly 64 km; the rest is not traced, so the totals here are a floor.

What it actually costs. There is no town between the two ends. There are long stretches with no fuel. There are stretches with no phone signal. The gradients are steeper than anything on 1095 and some of the seal has broken up. If something goes wrong here, it goes wrong somewhere that nobody is passing.

*Inference —* the recommendation this project would make, and it is a recommendation rather than a fact: take it on a trail bike or a midweight, in the dry, with a full tank, before noon, and not alone if that can be arranged. Take it on a 110 automatic only if you have already ridden Route 1095 and found it comfortable. In the rains, do not take it at all.

Provenance: harvested · s:mhs-measured
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:osm, s:wp-khun-yuam-district
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Route 107 (road/route-107)
Thai: ทางหลวงแผ่นดินหมายเลข 107

### what
Chiang Mai north towards Fang. The loop uses only its first stretch, as far as the Route 1095 turn near Mae Malai.

### story
*Inference —* the only thing to say about it is what it is for. It is a busy multi-lane road out of a city, it is the least interesting riding on the whole circuit, and it exists to get you to the junction. Ride it, do not judge the trip by it.

Route 1095 formerly began at Mae Malai market; since 1994 it begins at Ban Nong Khong on this road, which is the bypass. Both work; the signs use the new one.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:thwp-1095, s:wp-mae-taeng-district

## Route 108 (road/route-108)
Thai: ทางหลวงแผ่นดินหมายเลข 108

### what
Chiang Mai to Mae Hong Son the long way round: south through Hang Dong and Chom Thong to Hot, then west and north through Mae Sariang, Mae La Noi and Khun Yuam.

### story
The figures come from the Thai Wikipedia article and are worth carrying: about **350 kilometres** in total, in two halves. Chiang Mai to Hot is **88 kilometres** of four to six lanes with a median, narrowing to two lanes through the centres of Hang Dong, San Pa Tong, Thung Sieo and Chom Thong. Hot to Mae Hong Son is **265 kilometres** of two lanes the entire way, and the kilometre marks restart at zero at the Hot roundabout.

The article describes the mountain half exactly: it runs along steep hills as far as Mae Sariang, then parallels the Yuam river through Mae La Noi, climbs again past Ban Mae La Luang to Khun Yuam, and finally crosses the mountains to drop into Mae Hong Son town. It enters Mae Hong Son province at km 68+500 counting from Hot.

*Inference —* this is why counter-clockwise is a gentle start and clockwise is a gentle finish. Nothing on Route 108 asks anything sudden; it asks for stamina.

*Inference —* measured off the OpenStreetMap trace, 312.3 kilometres of Route 108 stitch into one run carrying 694 curves at a 25-degree threshold and 63 hairpins — 3.44 a kilometre. Half the density of Route 1095, over nearly twice the distance. That ratio is the whole difference between the two halves of this circuit.

Provenance: cited · s:thwp-108
Sources: s:thwp-108, s:mhs-measured, s:osm

## Route 1088 (road/route-1088)
Thai: ทางหลวงแผ่นดินหมายเลข 1088

### what
North out of Mae Chaem. Relevant to this circuit only as part of the 1263 shortcut's eastern exit.

### story
*Inference —* if you have taken the 1263 cut you arrive at Mae Chaem with a choice, and this is one arm of it: north and over the Doi Inthanon side before dropping to Chom Thong on Route 108. Measured off OSM the run is about 32 kilometres with 96 curves at a 25-degree threshold, ten of them hairpins.

It is high, it is cold in the morning, and it puts the highest point in Thailand within reach of a detour.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:wp-doi-inthanon, s:wp-mae-chaem-district

## Route 1095 (road/route-1095)
Thai: ทางหลวงแผ่นดินหมายเลข 1095

### what
Nong Khong on Route 107, over the hills to Pai, through Pangmapha, and down into Mae Hong Son. Sealed two lanes end to end. The most curve-dense long road on the circuit.

### story
Thai Wikipedia's article gives the route as Nong Khong to Mae Hong Son, two lanes both ways, and notes that it was formerly called the Mae Malai–Mae Hong Son highway and is still usually called the Mae Malai–Pai road. In 1994 a new alignment moved its start from Mae Malai market to Ban Nong Khong on Route 107, as a Mae Malai bypass; the old alignment became rural road Chiang Mai 3045. The spur into Pai town itself is Route 1395, leaving 1095 at km 96+035 and rejoining at km 99+303. The article describes the road as known for being winding, *กว่า 2,000 โค้ง* — more than 2,000 curves — and steep, and gives Chiang Mai to Mae Hong Son by this road as about 245 kilometres.

*Inference —* measured off the OpenStreetMap trace of the road, the longest stitched run of Route 1095 is 185 kilometres carrying 1,056 curves at a 25-degree threshold, 110 of them hairpins — about nearly six curves a kilometre, one every 254 metres. The section from Mae Malai to Pai alone carries 395. The method and its sensitivity are on /numbers/.

Provenance: cited · s:thwp-1095
Sources: s:thwp-1095, s:doh-1095, s:mhs-measured, s:osm

## Route 1096 (road/route-1096)
Thai: ทางหลวงแผ่นดินหมายเลข 1096

### what
Mae Rim to Samoeng, ridden as a day loop out of Chiang Mai and back. Not part of the Mae Hong Son circuit, and the best possible preparation for it.

### story
*Inference —* the case for riding this first is strong and almost nobody makes it. Measured off OSM the stitched run is 29.8 kilometres carrying 130 curves at a 25-degree threshold with 19 hairpins — **6.34 curves a kilometre, the densest road measured on this whole network**, against Route 1095's 5.71.

So it is the same riding, in a day, from a hotel you are already in, on a bike you have just rented, with Chiang Mai an hour away if something is wrong. A rider who finds the Samoeng loop tiring has learned something very cheap about what four days of it would be.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:wp-samoeng-district, s:wp-mae-rim-district

## Route 1263 (road/route-1263)
Thai: ทางหลวงแผ่นดินหมายเลข 1263

### what
Khun Yuam east to Mae Chaem. The shortcut that halves the loop, and the hardest riding in this network.

### story
*Inference —* the OpenStreetMap trace of this road comes back incomplete: 38.1 kilometres of it stitched, against the roughly 64 the road runs. Over the part that is mapped it carries 159 curves at a 25-degree threshold with 25 hairpins — **4.25 a kilometre, denser than Route 1095's 5.71** — on a third of 1095's length, with a fraction of the traffic. The rest of the road is not on this disk; treat the total as a floor.

What the numbers do not carry is the character: no town in between, long stretches with no fuel and no phone signal, gradients steeper than anything on 1095, and sections where the seal has broken up. It is the most rewarding road here and the one with the least margin.

*Inference —* in the rains it comes off most plans. Steep, broken seal, and nobody coming past for a while is a combination that stops being fun when it is also wet.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:osm, s:wp-khun-yuam-district, s:wp-mae-chaem-district

## Chiang Mai (town/chiang-mai)
Thai: เชียงใหม่

### what
The start and the finish. Both roads out of it — 107 to the north, 108 to the south — are the loop's two ends.

### story
*Inference —* the useful thing to say about Chiang Mai on a page about the loop is what it is for: rental, spares, a proper helmet if the shop's is bad, and the place the suitcase sits for four days.

One measured fact worth carrying out of town: across four burning seasons Chiang Mai's March mean PM2.5 is 37.8 µg/m³, higher than any town on the circuit. The air improves as you leave.

### today
Everything the rest of the circuit does not have: tyres in stock, a dealer for most brands, and a hospital that does not need a transfer.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-chiang-mai
Sources: s:wp-chiang-mai, s:open-meteo-aq

## Hot (town/hot)
Thai: ฮอด

### what
The hinge of the southern leg: east of here Route 108 is four to six lanes to Chiang Mai, west of here it is two lanes for 265 kilometres.

### story
The kilometre marks on Route 108 restart at zero at the Hot roundabout and run from there to Mae Hong Son — 265 kilometres. East of Hot to Chiang Mai is 88 kilometres of a different kind of road: four to six lanes with a median, narrowing to two through the town centres of Hang Dong, San Pa Tong, Thung Sieo and Chom Thong.

*Inference —* the practical meaning is that Hot is where the ride starts or ends, whichever way round you go. East of it you are commuting; west of it you are riding.

### today
Fuel, food, and the last four-lane road you will see for three days.

Provenance: cited · s:thwp-108
Sources: s:thwp-108, s:wp-hot-district

## Khun Yuam (town/khun-yuam)
Thai: ขุนยวม

### what
On Route 108 between Mae Hong Son and Mae La Noi, and the western end of the 1263 cut to Mae Chaem. Two reasons to stop, and both of them are specific.

### story
The first reason is Doi Mae U-Kho above the town, which turns yellow with *Tithonia diversifolia* in November.

The second is the war. Japanese forces used the route through this district during the Second World War, and the town holds a memorial hall to that period. *Inference —* what makes it worth the stop is not the military history but the domestic one: the relationship between a Thai town and the soldiers who came through it, which is a much less told story than the campaign.

Khun Yuam is also the junction where the loop can be halved. Route 1263 leaves here for Mae Chaem, 63 kilometres of the steepest and most curve-dense road in this whole network.

### today
Fuel, food, a bed, and the decision about whether to take the cut.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-khun-yuam-district
Sources: s:wp-khun-yuam-district, s:wp-thailand-in-world-war-ii, s:wp-tithonia-diversifolia

## Mae Chaem (town/mae-chaem)
Thai: แม่แจ่ม

### what
A Chiang Mai district in its own valley, reached from the loop only by Route 1263 or over the Inthanon massif.

### story
*Inference —* Mae Chaem is the town that turns the loop into a choice. Arriving here from Khun Yuam means the 1263 has been ridden and the circuit has been halved; the road on from here climbs over the Inthanon side and drops to Chom Thong on Route 108.

It is a weaving district and the cloth is its own subject, which this project has not yet written up.

### today
Small, and the services are small with it. Fill up in Khun Yuam before the cut, not here after it.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-mae-chaem-district
Sources: s:wp-mae-chaem-district, s:wp-doi-inthanon

## Mae Hong Son (town/mae-hong-son)
Thai: แม่ฮ่องสอน

### what
The far end of the loop and the only town on it with an airport, a hospital of size, and a chedi on a hill above the runway. Population small, altitude low, mountains on every side.

### story
Mae Hong Son province is the westernmost in Thailand and the most mountainous, 12,765 square kilometres at 22 people per square kilometre, the lowest population density of any province. As of 2012 it was also the poorest.

The province was formerly part of Mawkmai State, one of the Shan States, founded in 1767 by Hsai Khiao of a Chiang Mai noble family. The Anglo-Siamese Boundary Commission of 1892–93 ceded Mae Hong Son district to Siam while the trans-Salween districts stayed with British Burma — which is why the border runs where it does, and why the temples in town look Burmese rather than Lanna.

The town itself was established in the early nineteenth century as an elephant training camp, on the order of the then King of Chiang Mai. Shan people are the largest population group in the province; the other named groups are Karen, Lahu, Lisu, Lua, Miao and Pa-O, and Chinese Yunnanese. 77.5 per cent of inhabitants are Buddhist and 20.9 per cent Christian, which is a far higher Christian share than Thailand as a whole.

### today
For a rider it is the pivot: the point where the loop turns, the one place with a hospital and a full range of mechanics, and the town that deserves two nights rather than one. The dawn mist that gives the province its nickname is best seen from the chedi on the hill, which means being up before the town is.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-mae-hong-son-province
Sources: s:wp-mae-hong-son-province, s:wp-mae-hong-son, s:wp-mueang-mae-hong-son-district, s:wp-shan-state, s:air4thai

## Mae Sariang (town/mae-sariang)
Thai: แม่สะเรียง

### what
The largest town on the southern leg and the natural overnight between Mae Hong Son and Chiang Mai. Teak-era shophouses, Burmese-style wats, and a river.

### story
Mae Sariang district reaches west to the Salween, which is the border, and the road on to Mae Sam Laep is the way to see it.

*Inference —* the reason to give Mae Sariang a night rather than treating it as a lunch stop is arithmetic. Mae Hong Son to Chiang Mai in one day by Route 108 is a very long day on a mountain road; broken at Mae Sariang it is two comfortable ones. Riders on a tight schedule push through and arrive after dark, which is the single most avoidable mistake on this circuit.

### today
Quiet, cheap, and the last town of any size before the long empty run north or the long fast run east.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-mae-sariang-district
Sources: s:wp-mae-sariang-district, s:wp-salween-river, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province

## Pai (town/pai)
Thai: ปาย

### what
Night one clockwise. A small district town in a flat river basin ringed by hills, with more guesthouses, coffee and motorcycle rental per head than anywhere else on the circuit.

### story
Pai sits on the Pai river in a basin at around 480 metres, which is the thing that explains both the climate and the smoke: cool air pools here at night, and so does everything else in the air.

What it is now is contested locally in the ordinary way, and this page reports the argument rather than joining it. *Inference —* what is not in dispute is the practical picture for a rider: it is the best-supplied town on the northern leg, it has mechanics who see foreign bikes daily, and it is the one place on the circuit where a room can be hard to find without booking in the cool season.

### today
The measured air here is the mildest of the circuit in March — a 26.1 µg/m³ monthly mean against Chiang Mai's 37.8 — and the province's single air monitor is a hundred kilometres away in Mae Hong Son, so nobody official is measuring it.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-pai-district
Sources: s:wp-pai-thailand, s:wp-pai-district, s:wp-pai-river, s:open-meteo-aq

## Soppong (town/soppong)
Thai: สบป่อง

### what
The main settlement of Pang Mapha district, in limestone karst country. Officially Pang Mapha; on the road signs and in every conversation, Soppong.

### story
Pang Mapha district is limestone, and limestone here means caves — the district holds a large number of them, including the one at Tham Lot with its river running through.

*Inference —* for a rider Soppong is the answer to a specific problem: the Pai to Mae Hong Son run is long enough to be a poor half-day and short enough to be a wasted full one, and Soppong sits in the middle of it. Staying here rather than pushing on buys you the caves in the morning light and takes the hardest descent off the end of a long day.

### today
Fuel, food, a few guesthouses, and no more than that. Treat the pump here as the last certain one before Mae Hong Son.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-pang-mapha-district
Sources: s:wp-pang-mapha-district, s:wp-tham-lot-cave

## Ban Rak Thai (stop/ban-rak-thai)
Thai: บ้านรักไทย

### what
A village north of Mae Hong Son settled by Chinese Yunnanese, on a reservoir, with tea terraces and the border immediately behind it.

### story
Chinese Yunnanese are one of the named population groups of Mae Hong Son province. *Inference —* this village is the most visible expression of that on the circuit: the food is Yunnanese, the tea is grown on the slopes above, and the architecture is not Thai.

It is a dead end. The road goes there and comes back, which means an afternoon out of Mae Hong Son rather than a leg of the loop — and which is a large part of why a rider should give Mae Hong Son two nights.

*Inference —* the altitude and the water make it cold in the mornings in the cool season in a way the valley is not.

Provenance: cited · s:thwp-ban-rak-thai
Sources: s:thwp-ban-rak-thai, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Doi Inthanon (stop/doi-inthanon)
Thai: ดอยอินทนนท์

### what
2,565 metres, in Chom Thong district, reached from Route 108 or from Mae Chaem over Route 1088. Not on the loop; one turn off it.

### story
The summit is the highest point in Thailand and sits in a national park. The road up is sealed the whole way and steep in places.

*Inference —* on this circuit it is a decision about a day rather than about a mountain. Clockwise it lands near the end, at Chom Thong, when you are nearly home and tired; counter-clockwise it lands on day one, when you are fresh but have a long way to go. Either way it is a full extra day to do properly, and a rushed half-day gets you a car park in cloud.

A rider coming over the 1263 cut can reach it from the Mae Chaem side on Route 1088, which is the quieter approach.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-doi-inthanon
Sources: s:wp-doi-inthanon, s:wp-chom-thong

## Huai Nam Dang (stop/huai-nam-dang)
Thai: ห้วยน้ำดัง

### what
A national park straddling the Chiang Mai and Mae Hong Son line, right on Route 1095, with a viewpoint that looks east over cloud at dawn.

### story
*Inference —* the rare one on this circuit that is directly on the route rather than up a dead end, which matters because a dawn viewpoint you have to detour to is a dawn you will not see.

The mist is a cool-season, still-air, before-sunrise phenomenon — the same conditions that make Pang Ung work, a hundred kilometres west. From here the sun comes up over the ridges toward Chiang Mai with cloud filling the valleys underneath.

*Inference —* the arrangement that works is sleeping near the top rather than riding up from Pai in the dark. There is camping and there are park bungalows.

**Not on this disk:** current fees, bungalow booking or road conditions to the viewpoint.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-mae-taeng-district, s:wp-pai-district, s:osm
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## The Japanese memorial at Khun Yuam (stop/khun-yuam-memorial)
Thai: อนุสรณ์สถานมิตรภาพไทย–ญี่ปุ่น ขุนยวม

### what
A memorial hall in Khun Yuam holding material from the Japanese presence in this district during the Second World War.

### story
Thailand's position in the Second World War was its own complicated thing — an alliance under pressure, an occupation that was not called one, and a resistance movement inside the government. Japanese forces moved through northern Thailand toward and from Burma, and Khun Yuam was on one of those routes.

*Inference —* what makes this worth a stop on a motorcycle trip is that it is a local record rather than a national one: what is kept here is the relationship between a small Thai town and the soldiers who passed through it, including the ones who did not leave. That is a different subject from the campaign, and it is much less often told.

**Not on this disk:** the hall's current opening hours, its admission charge, or the exact composition of its collection. This project has not verified them.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-thailand-in-world-war-ii
Sources: s:wp-thailand-in-world-war-ii, s:wp-japanese-occupation-of-burma, s:wp-khun-yuam-district
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Mae Sam Laep and the Salween (stop/mae-sam-laep)
Thai: แม่สามแลบ และแม่น้ำสาละวิน

### what
A river village west of Mae Sariang at the end of a side road, on the Salween where it forms the frontier.

### story
The Salween rises in Tibet and runs some two and a half thousand kilometres to the Andaman Sea, and for a long stretch of its lower course it is the line between Thailand and Myanmar. At Mae Sam Laep you are standing on that line.

*Inference —* this is the best detour on the southern leg and almost nobody takes it, because the long Mae Sariang day already feels long. It is worth rearranging the day for: a wide brown river, forest on both banks, longtail boats loading rice and people, and a far bank that is a different country with no bridge to it.

The road in is a side road off Route 108 and it descends steeply to the water. *Inference —* go in the morning, when the boats are working, and eat at the river.

**Not on this disk:** current boat services, prices, or whether any particular trip is running. The border is a live administrative thing and what is possible there changes.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-salween-river
Sources: s:wp-salween-river, s:wp-mae-sariang-district, s:thwp-salween
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Mae Surin Waterfall (stop/mae-surin-waterfall)
Thai: น้ำตกแม่สุรินทร์

### what
A single-drop waterfall in Namtok Mae Surin National Park, in Khun Yuam district.

### story
The national park is named after it and also contains the Doi Mae U-Kho hillside where the *Tithonia* blooms in November, so a single detour off Route 108 near Khun Yuam can reach both.

*Inference —* the waterfall is a rains-and-just-after phenomenon like every waterfall; by March there is much less of it. The bloom is the opposite, in November. The two reasons to go up there do not coincide.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-namtok-mae-surin-national-park
Sources: s:wp-namtok-mae-surin-national-park, s:wp-khun-yuam-district
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Op Luang (stop/op-luang)
Thai: ออบหลวง

### what
A gorge on the Chaem river in a national park on Route 108, roughly midway between Hot and Mae Sariang.

### story
*Inference —* the practical value of this place on a long empty leg is that it exists. The Mae Sariang to Hot run is the emptiest on the circuit, and a gorge with a car park, shade and a bridge over it is the natural break in the middle of three hours.

The gorge itself is narrow and deep and the water goes through it fast; the national park around it covers a much larger area of hill forest.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-op-luang-national-park
Sources: s:wp-op-luang-national-park

## Pa Bong Piang rice terraces (stop/pa-bong-piang)
Thai: นาขั้นบันไดป่าบงเปียง

### what
In Mae Chaem district, off the eastern end of the 1263 cut. One of the reasons to take the shortcut at all.

### story
*Tradition holds —* these are working Karen terraces, farmed, not a viewing platform. They are at their green between about July and September and turn gold before the harvest around October and November.

*Inference —* the timing is the opposite of most of this circuit's advice. The cool dry season that everyone books is when the terraces are cut stubble. If the terraces are what you came for, come in the green season — which is also, from the air data, the cleanest air of the year.

Getting there is a side road off the Mae Chaem end, and it is the kind of place where arriving early means having it to yourself.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:wp-mae-chaem-district, s:osm, s:wp-karen-peoples
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Pai Canyon (stop/pai-canyon)
Thai: กองแลน

### what
Kong Lan: narrow eroded sandstone ridges on the edge of the Pai basin, walked at sunset by most of the town.

### story
*Inference —* ten minutes from Pai on Route 1095, which makes it the last stop of the day you ride in rather than an outing of its own. Go for sunset: the light comes in sideways along the ridges and the whole basin turns orange underneath you.

The ridges are narrow with open drops on both sides and the sandstone is soft. Walk out as far as you feel like and no further — the view from the first fifty metres is the same view.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-pai-district, s:wp-pai-thailand
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## The evening in Pai (stop/pai-walking-street)
Thai: ถนนคนเดินปาย

### what
Pai's evening market runs down the main street every night in the season: food stalls, music, and most of the town's visitors in one place.

### story
*Inference —* this is the most divisive thing on the circuit and it is worth saying plainly what it is. Pai in high season is busy, loud, young and commercial. Wikipedia's article records that between November and March the town has traffic jams and runs short of electricity, water and petrol.

If that is what you want for one night, it is genuinely good at it: the food is cheap and various, there is live music most nights, and the valley is still right there in the morning.

If it is not what you want, the answer is not to skip Pai — it is to sleep outside the town in the valley, come in for dinner, and ride out early. Soppong, forty minutes on, is the opposite of all of this.

*Tradition holds —* the night market is a Thai form, not a visitor invention. Every town on this loop has an evening market; Pai's is simply the one with an audience.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-pai-thailand
Sources: s:wp-pai-thailand, s:wp-night-market, s:osm

## Pang Ung (stop/pang-ung)
Thai: ปางอุ๋ง

### what
A royal-project reservoir in the hills north-west of Mae Hong Son, reached by the same road system as Ban Rak Thai.

### story
*Inference —* this is a dawn place and it is only a dawn place. The mist that makes it worth the ride is a cool-season, early-morning, still-air phenomenon, and at ten in the morning it is a reservoir with pine trees.

Which has a scheduling consequence that runs through this whole site: it requires sleeping within reach of it, which means two nights in Mae Hong Son, which means the four-day loop is really a five-day loop if you want the things Mae Hong Son is actually known for.

**Not on this disk:** current access arrangements, charges or camping rules.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-mueang-mae-hong-son-district, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Su Tong Pae bridge (stop/su-tong-pae)
Thai: สะพานซูตองเป้

### what
A long bamboo bridge over rice fields and a stream outside Mae Hong Son town, on the route toward Khun Yuam.

### story
*Tradition holds —* the bridge was built so that monks from the monastery on one side could walk on alms round to the village on the other without crossing the fields and the water, and the villagers built it with them. The bamboo is replaced as it wears.

*Inference —* for a rider it is the right kind of stop, which is to say it takes fifteen minutes and it is on the way rather than up a dead end. Early morning is when the alms round happens and it is a working bridge at that hour, not a viewpoint.

**Not on this disk:** whether an admission or donation is now collected, and the bridge's current condition.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-mueang-mae-hong-son-district
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Tham Lot (stop/tham-lot)
Thai: ถ้ำลอด

### what
A limestone cave in Pang Mapha district with the Nam Lang stream running through it. Entered by lamp and by bamboo raft, with a local guide.

### story
The cave carries prehistoric material — wooden coffins of the kind the district is known for — as well as the river. *Tradition holds —* visitors are taken through by local guides with pressure lamps, and the raft sections are poled.

*Inference —* the reason to sleep in Soppong rather than push on is largely this: the cave wants a couple of hours and morning is when the guides and the light are both there.

At dusk a very large roost of birds and bats exchanges places at the entrance, which is a spectacle that costs nothing and needs you to be there at the right hour rather than to pay for anything.

### today
A national park fee applies and Thailand charges foreigners a separate rate; the guide and lamp are a separate, locally set charge. Neither figure is printed here because neither was verified on the build date.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-tham-lot-cave
Sources: s:wp-tham-lot-cave, s:wp-pang-mapha-district
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Tham Pla, the fish cave (stop/tham-pla)
Thai: ถ้ำปลา

### what
A spring-fed pool at a cave mouth north of Mae Hong Son town, in its own national park, holding a resident population of large barb.

### story
The park is Tham Pla–Namtok Pha Suea National Park, which also holds the Pha Suea waterfall further north near the border.

*Tradition holds —* the fish are not taken, and that is the reason there are so many of them and they are that size. *Inference —* the place is a short ride from Mae Hong Son on the road toward Ban Rak Thai, which makes it a natural first stop on a day spent north of town rather than a destination in itself.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-tham-pla-namtok-pha-suea-national-park
Sources: s:wp-tham-pla-namtok-pha-suea-national-park, s:wp-mueang-mae-hong-son-district
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Wat Chong Kham and Wat Chong Klang (wat/chong-kham-chong-klang)
Thai: วัดจองคำ และวัดจองกลาง

### what
The pair of Shan-Burmese temples on Nong Chong Kham, the pond at the centre of Mae Hong Son town.

### story
*Inference —* the tiered roofs, the tin, the fretwork and the whitewash are all Shan and Burmese rather than Lanna, and the reason is the border: this town was on the Shan side of a line that was drawn in the 1890s.

*Tradition holds —* Wat Chong Klang holds a set of painted glass panels and carved figures brought from Burma, on Buddhist narrative subjects.

The practical note for a rider: this is a two-minute walk from anywhere in the town centre, it is free, and the hour that makes it is after dark, when both are lit and the pond does the work. It is the reason an evening in Mae Hong Son is not wasted.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-mae-hong-son
Sources: s:wp-mae-hong-son, s:wp-shan-people, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Wat Phra That Doi Kong Mu (wat/doi-kong-mu)
Thai: วัดพระธาตุดอยกองมู

### what
The temple on the hill west of Mae Hong Son town. Two Shan-style chedis, a road to the top, and the view that gives the province its nickname.

### story
*Inference —* the architecture is the province's history in one object. Mae Hong Son was Shan before it was Thai — part of Mawkmai, one of the Shan States, until the Anglo-Siamese boundary settlement of 1892–93 — and the chedis here are Shan and Burmese in form rather than Lanna. A rider who has come from Chiang Mai has spent three days looking at Lanna wats and arrives at something that is plainly not one.

The practical note: there is a road to the top, so this is a ride rather than a climb, and the reason to be there is the hour rather than the building. 'City of three mists' is a description of what is visible from up here before the sun gets to work.

Provenance: cited · s:thwp-wat-phra-that-doi-kong-mu
Sources: s:thwp-wat-phra-that-doi-kong-mu, s:wp-mae-hong-son, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province, s:wp-shan-state

## Why the temples here are called Chong (wat/jong-and-chong)
Thai: ทำไมวัดแถบนี้ชื่อจอง

### what
A naming pattern that maps the cultural border better than the political one does, and it is visible in the map data.

### story
*Tradition holds —* *chong* or *jong* (จอง) is the Shan word for a monastery, and it turns up in temple names through Shan country on both sides of the border.

**So it should be testable, and it is.** Counting the named Buddhist temples in the OpenStreetMap harvest within fifteen kilometres of each town: Mae Hong Son has three of ten carrying the word — Wat Chong Kham, Wat Chong Klang and the pair listed together as วัดจองกลาง วัดจองคำ. Mae Sariang has one, Wat Jong Soong. Khun Yuam has none. Pai has none of seventeen. **Chiang Mai has none of three hundred and eighty-two.**

*Inference —* that is a small sample and OpenStreetMap's romanisation is inconsistent, so treat it as a floor rather than a survey. But zero out of 382 in Chiang Mai against three out of ten in Mae Hong Son is not noise, and it is the same line the architecture draws: this province was Shan before it was Thai, and the Anglo-Siamese boundary settlement of 1892–93 moved the border without moving the people.

Which means a rider crossing from Pai to Mae Hong Son is crossing something older than the province, and the temple signboards are where it shows.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:osm, s:wp-shan-people, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province, s:wp-shan-state
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Wat Hua Wiang (wat/wat-hua-wiang)
Thai: วัดหัวเวียง

### what
In the centre of Mae Hong Son town, beside the morning market. The image inside is the reason to go in.

### story
*Tradition holds —* the principal image, Phra Chao Phara La Khaeng, is held to have been cast in Burma and brought over in sections. Whatever the exact route, the object is not a Lanna casting and it does not look like one.

*Inference —* what makes this one worth ten minutes rather than a photograph from the road is the setting. It is a working neighbourhood temple in the middle of a market, with a corrugated roof and no ticket, which is a different proposition from a hilltop chedi, and it is where you see what these buildings are for on an ordinary Tuesday.

It is next to the morning market, which means you can do both before eight and be riding by nine.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-mae-hong-son, s:osm, s:wp-shan-people
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Wat Jong Soong (wat/wat-jong-soong)
Thai: วัดจองสูง

### what
In the middle of Mae Sariang, with the whitewashed tiered chedis and the tin roofs of the Shan-Burmese manner rather than the Lanna one.

### story
*Inference —* Mae Sariang is the southern Shan town on this circuit, and this temple is the clearest single piece of evidence for that. From here south and east the architecture turns Lanna; from here north and west it stays Shan all the way to the border.

OpenStreetMap maps eighteen named temples within fifteen kilometres of Mae Sariang. This is the only one carrying the Shan word, which is a smaller share than Mae Hong Son's three in ten — the pattern thins as you go south, which is what you would expect of a cultural gradient rather than a line.

*Inference —* for a rider it is a five-minute stop in the middle of a town you are probably sleeping in anyway, on the longest and emptiest leg of the circuit. It is the leg that most needs a reason to slow down.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:osm, s:wp-mae-sariang-district, s:wp-shan-people
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Wat Phra That Mae Yen (wat/wat-phra-that-mae-yen)
Thai: วัดพระธาตุแม่เย็น

### what
On the hill east of Pai. The seated white image is visible from most of the town, and the climb is the reason people go.

### story
*Inference —* the useful thing about this one is the timing. It faces west over the valley, which makes it a sunset rather than a sunrise, and it is close enough to town that it works on the evening you arrive rather than needing its own morning.

There is a road up as well as the steps. On a small bike take the road; the steps are the point only if you want them to be.

This is a Lanna-named temple — *Phra That*, a relic stupa — in a town that sits on the Shan side of the province, which is a reminder that the naming pattern further west is a tendency and not a rule. Pai has none of the Chong names at all.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-pai-thailand, s:wp-pai-district, s:osm
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Grilled by the road (dish/grilled-by-the-road)
Thai: ของย่างริมทาง

### what
The roadside grill is the most reliable good meal between towns, and you smell it before you see it.

### story
*Tradition holds —* *gai yang* is chicken butterflied flat, clamped in split bamboo and grilled slowly over charcoal at the roadside; it goes with sticky rice and *som tam*, green papaya pounded with lime, chilli, fish sauce and tomato. Pork skewers, grilled river fish packed in salt, and sausages are on the same grills.

*Inference —* the smell is the point. On a bike you get it a hundred metres before the stall, which is enough warning to stop, and it is the single most common reason a planned four-hour leg becomes five.

*Tradition holds —* the northern sausage, *sai ua*, is the local one: pork with lemongrass, galangal, makrut leaf and chilli, coiled and grilled. It is sold by weight at every market on this circuit and it travels in a bag on the bike better than anything else here.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-thai-cuisine, s:wp-nam-phrik

## Khao soi (dish/khao-soi)
Thai: ข้าวซอย

### what
A coconut curry noodle soup of upper northern Thailand, Laos and the Shan States. Chicken or beef, pickled mustard greens, shallot, lime, chilli paste on the side.

### story
The name means *cut rice*, from the way the fresh sheets of noodle are sliced. It belongs to the Tai Yai and to the wider Burmese-border kitchen as much as to Chiang Mai, which is why it is on the board the whole way round this loop.

*Inference —* the practical fact for a rider is the hour. This is breakfast and lunch food. Many of the best places sell out and close by early afternoon, so it is a reason to be on the road by seven and off it by one — which happens to be the same advice the smoke and the heat give you, for entirely different reasons.

*Tradition holds —* the four things on the side are not a garnish. The pickled greens and the lime cut the coconut, the shallot is raw and sharp, and the chilli paste is where the heat lives, so the bowl arrives mild and you build it.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-khao-soi
Sources: s:wp-khao-soi, s:wp-thai-cuisine

## The morning market (dish/morning-market)
Thai: ตลาดเช้า

### what
Every town on this loop has one. Rice, curries in bags, grilled things, sticky rice, coffee, and whatever the hills sent down that morning.

### story
*Inference —* this is the single best thing on the circuit that costs almost nothing and that most riders sleep through. The market is at its fullest between five and seven and is packing up by nine, which is the same window in which you want to be riding anyway — so the answer is to eat first and leave at eight, not to lie in and buy a sandwich.

What is on the tables changes by altitude and by who is selling. In Mae Hong Son and Mae Sariang the Shan and Burmese side of the kitchen is right there; up the hill it is Karen and Lisu produce; in Mae Chaem it is a Lanna market.

*Tradition holds —* curry is sold by the bag, tied at the neck, to take away. You buy rice separately. Nobody minds you pointing.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-night-market, s:wp-thai-cuisine, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province

## Kanom jeen nam ngiao (dish/nam-ngiao)
Thai: ขนมจีนน้ำเงี้ยว

### what
Fermented rice vermicelli under a thin, sour, red broth of tomato and pork, with dried kapok flower, pork blood cubes and a pork rib.

### story
The name is the giveaway: *ngiao* is an old Thai word for the Shan. This is Shan food that northern Thailand adopted, and on the western half of this loop you are eating it where it comes from rather than where it travelled to.

*Tradition holds —* the dried kapok flower, *dok ngiao*, is the ingredient that makes it what it is: it goes soft in the broth and adds body rather than flavour. Without it the bowl is a tomato soup.

*Inference —* it is lighter than khao soi and served all day, which makes it the better bet when you arrive somewhere at three in the afternoon and the khao soi has gone.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-thai-cuisine, s:wp-shan-people
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Sticky rice (dish/sticky-rice)
Thai: ข้าวเหนียว

### what
Glutinous rice, steamed rather than boiled, eaten with the right hand in small pressed balls. The everyday grain of the north and the northeast.

### story
Glutinous rice contains effectively no amylose, which is the starch that makes ordinary rice separate into grains; that is the whole reason it holds together.

*Inference —* why it matters on a motorcycle: a basket of sticky rice and a bag of something to dip it in needs no plate, no cutlery, no table and no stop longer than the time it takes to sit down. It is the only lunch on this list you can genuinely eat at a viewpoint.

*Tradition holds —* you take a small amount, press it into a ball in your fingers, and use it to pick up whatever is beside it. It is eaten with the hand and it is not rude to do so.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-glutinous-rice
Sources: s:wp-glutinous-rice, s:wp-thai-cuisine

## Thua nao (dish/thua-nao)
Thai: ถั่วเน่า

### what
Soybeans fermented, mashed, pressed flat and sun-dried into thin discs, then toasted or fried and crumbled into food. The name means rotten bean and nobody minds.

### story
*Tradition holds —* this is the northern and Shan answer to fish sauce, in a region far from the sea. Where central Thailand reaches for *nam pla*, the hill kitchens reach for a toasted disc of fermented bean.

*Inference —* it is the single ingredient that most reliably tells you which side of the cultural line you are eating on, and it is easy to miss because it arrives crumbled into something else. Ask, and people will show you the discs — they are stacked like coasters in every market on the western half of this loop.

The smell on a toasting grill is strong and it is the good kind.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-soybean, s:wp-burmese-cuisine, s:wp-shan-people
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## The Yunnanese table at Ban Rak Thai (dish/yunnan-table)
Thai: อาหารยูนนานที่บ้านรักไทย

### what
Chinese Yunnanese food, on a reservoir, a few kilometres from the Myanmar border, at the end of a road that goes nowhere else.

### story
Chinese Yunnanese are one of the named population groups of Mae Hong Son province, and this village is the most concentrated expression of that on the circuit: the cooking is Yunnanese, not Thai, and so is the architecture.

*Inference —* for a rider the thing worth knowing is that it is a dead-end road, so this is an afternoon out of Mae Hong Son rather than a leg of the loop. Which is a large part of why Mae Hong Son is worth two nights and not one.

*Tradition holds —* the tea is grown on the terraces above the village and is sold and poured by the people who picked it. That is the meal, as much as the food is.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-yunnan-cuisine
Sources: s:wp-yunnan-cuisine, s:thwp-ban-rak-thai, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Miang and mountain tea (coffee/miang-and-tea)
Thai: เมี่ยงและชาบนดอย

### what
Before the coffee, these hills grew tea. Much of it still does, and the older use of the leaf is not a drink at all.

### story
*Tradition holds —* *miang* is tea leaf steamed and fermented, then chewed as a wad with salt, ginger or sugar. It was the northern Thai way with the tea plant long before anyone here brewed it, and *miang* forests — old semi-wild tea gardens under shade trees — still stand on these hills.

*Inference —* the reason it is worth knowing is that it reframes what you are riding through. The coffee on these slopes arrived in the twentieth century as a substitution crop; the tea has been here far longer, and the shade trees over the old gardens are why parts of this forest look tended rather than wild.

At Ban Rak Thai the Yunnanese grow and brew tea in the Chinese manner and will pour it for you properly, which is a different plant culture again, arriving over the border from the north.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-thai-cuisine, s:wp-coffee-production-in-thailand, s:wp-yunnan-cuisine
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Arabica off the ridge you just rode over (coffee/ridge-arabica)
Thai: อาราบิก้าจากดอยที่เพิ่งข้ามมา

### what
Northern Thailand grows arabica on the hills this road climbs. The plant wants altitude, shade and a dry harvest — which is exactly what these slopes are.

### story
*Coffea arabica* does best at altitude in the tropics, and the reason there is coffee on these hills at all is a deliberate substitution: Thai highland coffee was promoted from the 1970s onward as a replacement crop for opium poppy, under royal project and government programmes.

*Inference —* which makes a roadside cup on this circuit a piece of the region's history rather than a nice drink, and it is why so many of the growers are Lisu, Lahu, Akha, Hmong and Karen families rather than lowland Thai companies.

What this means on the road: the cup at the top of a climb is often grown within sight of where you are standing. Ask where it is from and you frequently get pointed at a hillside rather than given a brand.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-coffee-production-in-thailand
Sources: s:wp-coffee-production-in-thailand, s:wp-coffea-arabica

## The stall at the top of the climb (coffee/roadside-stall)
Thai: เพิงกาแฟบนยอดดอย

### what
Somewhere near the top of most long climbs on this circuit there is a shack selling coffee, with a bench pointed at the valley.

### story
*Inference —* this is the thing to plan the day around. The distance is short and the day is long, and these stops are why.

The pattern is consistent enough to rely on. A climb of any length on 1095, 1263 or 1088 will have a pull-in near the top where the view opens, and where there is a view there is usually someone selling coffee. The coffee is often grown nearby; the view is always free.

**What the harvest found:** OpenStreetMap has 220 cafés mapped within twelve kilometres of a town on this loop, 188 of them named. That is a floor and not a survey — the shack with three stools and no sign is exactly the kind of place a volunteer mapper has not entered.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-coffee-production-in-thailand, s:osm

## The 7-Eleven (coffee/seven-eleven)
Thai: เซเว่น

### what
In the towns, the convenience store is a coffee stop, a water stop, a shade stop and a toilet. It is also the most reliable of the four.

### story
*Inference —* there is a kind of rider who will ride past a 7-Eleven in forty-degree heat because it is not characterful. That rider arrives at the guesthouse dehydrated, and dehydration on a bike arrives without a signal because the airflow stops you noticing you are sweating.

What it is good for: cold water in quantity, shade with air conditioning in it, a toilet that is always there, an ATM, a phone top-up, and coffee that is fine.

What it is not good for is the reason you came. Between the towns, stop at the stall with the bench and the view. In the towns, at two in the afternoon, in March, take the air conditioning.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-thai-cuisine

## Pha Bong hot springs (spring/pha-bong)
Thai: น้ำพุร้อนผาบ่อง

### what
A developed hot spring on the southern road out of Mae Hong Son, with a communal foot pool and rooms where the water is run into a tub for you.

### story
*Inference —* this one is on the route rather than up a side road, which on a circuit where every detour costs daylight is most of what makes it usable. It is the first thing on Route 108 going south, so it works as a stop on the way out of Mae Hong Son rather than an expedition.

*Tradition holds —* the private room with a tub is the arrangement at Thai developed springs, and it is what to ask for if sitting in a communal pool in a swimsuit is not what you want. A foot pool costs less and does most of the work.

**Not on this disk:** current charges or hours.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:wp-hot-spring, s:wp-mueang-mae-hong-son-district, s:osm
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## Tha Pai hot springs (spring/tha-pai-hot-springs)
Thai: น้ำพุร้อนท่าปาย

### what
A hot spring inside a national park east of Pai, where the source feeds a stream you can sit in where it has cooled enough.

### story
A hot spring is groundwater heated at depth and returned to the surface, and in this part of northern Thailand there are several along the same geological grain the road follows.

*Inference —* arrive in Pai with daylight left and this is where the afternoon goes. Teak overhead, the stream running warm over your legs, and nothing else to do until dinner.

**Not on this disk:** the current entrance fee — Thailand charges a separate foreigner rate at national parks — the opening hours, or which pools are open in which season. The source is very hot; the temperature you can sit in is a stretch of the stream, not the source itself.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:wp-hot-spring, s:wp-pai-district, s:osm
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## How a Thai hot spring works (spring/what-a-spring-is)
Thai: น้ำพุร้อนแบบไทยเป็นอย่างไร

### what
What to expect at a developed spring here, and how it differs from the Japanese arrangement most visitors have in mind.

### story
An onsen is bathed in naked, sex-segregated, after washing. *Tradition holds —* a Thai developed spring is generally not that: communal pools are mixed and clothed, swimwear or a sarong, and the built form is usually concrete pools and a foot bath rather than timber and stone.

The private room with a tub is the option if you want to be alone, and it is normally cheap.

*Tradition holds —* the egg thing is not a gimmick for visitors. Baskets of raw eggs are sold at the source and lowered into it; the water is hot enough to cook them and people have been doing it as long as there have been eggs and springs.

*Inference —* what none of that changes is the reason to go. Hot water, a hillside, and an hour in which nothing is required of you. It is the cheapest hour on the circuit and it is not close.

Provenance: tradition
Sources: s:wp-hot-spring, s:wp-onsen

## The hut with no wall on the valley side (stay/bamboo-hut)
Thai: กระท่อมที่ไม่มีผนังด้านหุบเขา

### what
The form that made Pai's name and has since spread down the whole circuit: a raised bamboo platform hut, open on the view side, often with the bathroom in a separate box.

### story
*Inference —* what you are buying is the first ten minutes after you stop riding, when you sit on the step with the engine ticking as it cools and the valley doing whatever the valley is doing. On a trip whose whole subject is motion, the places that make stopping worth something are doing the heavier work.

Two things worth knowing. It is cold before dawn from November to February and bamboo is not insulated, so the blanket matters more than the view does at five in the morning. And the huts with the best view are usually up the steepest track — the one at the bottom of the slope looks at the same valley.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:osm, s:wp-pai-district

## The teak shophouse (stay/teak-shophouse)
Thai: ตึกแถวไม้สัก

### what
Mae Sariang and Mae Hong Son both keep rows of timber shophouses from the teak years, and some of them take guests.

### story
Teak built these towns. The trade ran west into Burma and down the rivers, and the buildings that are left are the physical remains of it — wide boards, deep eaves, a balcony over the shopfront.

*Inference —* staying in one is the cheapest history lesson on the circuit, and the trade-off is plain: timber carries sound, so you will hear the street until it sleeps and the stairs whenever anyone uses them. Mae Sariang is the quieter of the two towns to try it in.

The rooms are usually simple — a bed, a fan, a shared bathroom in the older ones. What you get is the building.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-teak
Sources: s:wp-teak, s:wp-mae-sariang-district, s:osm

## Where to put the nights (stay/where-to-put-the-nights)
Thai: ควรนอนที่ไหนบ้าง

### what
Which towns are worth a night, which are worth two, and the one decision that changes the trip most.

### story
*Inference —* the single highest-value change anyone can make to this itinerary is **two nights in Mae Hong Son instead of one.** Everything the province is actually known for is a dawn or an afternoon that a one-night stop cannot reach: the mist off Doi Kong Mu before the town wakes, Pang Ung at six in the morning, the dead-end road up to Ban Rak Thai, the lake temples lit after dark. One night gets you an evening and a departure.

**Second-highest:** stopping at Soppong rather than running Pai to Mae Hong Son in a day. It turns a long day ending in the hardest descent of the northern leg into two short ones with a cave in the middle.

**Worth a night:** Pai, Soppong, Mae Hong Son, Mae Sariang. **Worth two:** Mae Hong Son, and Pai if you want the valley rather than the town. **Skip if pushed:** Khun Yuam and Hot are stops, not stays, unless the Bua Tong is out.

**What the harvest found:** 417 places to stay are mapped within twelve kilometres of a town on this loop, 402 of them named. Pai has 259 of them and Soppong has 7, which tells you most of what you need to know about booking ahead in each.

Provenance: harvested · s:osm
Sources: s:osm, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province

## Annoyances (hazard/annoyances)
Thai: เรื่องกวนใจ

### what
The small stuff, in one drawer, with what to do about it and what to say afterwards. None of these will end your trip. Most of them will end up being the bit you tell people about.

### story
**Village dogs** — One comes off a porch at your ankle.

*Antidote —* Slow, hold a straight line, keep going. It is defending a boundary, not hunting, and the chase ends in a few metres. The swerve is the only part that can hurt you.

*Alibi —* Every rider in Thailand has this story. Yours is not the best one.

**The guesthouse driveway** — Six hundred kilometres survived, and it goes over outside the room.

*Antidote —* Stop at the bottom and look before committing. Take the luggage off if it is steep. Walk it if the concrete is wet — polished wet concrete is far more slippery than it looks. On anything heavy, reverse in.

*Alibi —* At walking pace, with a bag on, on wet concrete, at the end of a six-hour day. Nobody who has ridden here will raise an eyebrow.

**A loaded bike steers differently** — It goes where it was pointed a second ago.

*Antidote —* Low and forward: footwell before rack, rack before pillion seat, heavy things against the tank. A rucksack on your back is the worst option of all because it moves when you do.

*Alibi —* Or send the bag ahead and ride the bike the shop designed.

**The pump is shut** — You arrive at four and the village station closed at three.

*Antidote —* Fill at every town whether or not the tank needs it. Where there is no station, small shops sell fuel by the litre from bottles on a rack outside.

*Alibi —* The bottle costs a little more and comes with someone who wants to know where you are going.

**No signal** — The map stops working somewhere on the 1263.

*Antidote —* Download the offline map before you leave the guesthouse wifi. The road is one road; the kilometre stones tell you where you are.

*Alibi —* Two hours without a phone on a mountain road is the thing you told people you came for.

**The afternoon storm** — It arrives at two, hard, for forty minutes.

*Antidote —* Stop. Have the coffee. In the green season the rain is heavy and short, and a day planned to finish at two usually finishes dry.

*Alibi —* The forty minutes under a shop awning with three other people waiting it out is a better story than the kilometres either side of it.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-motorcycle-safety, s:mhs-measured

## Brake fade (hazard/brake-fade)
Thai: เบรกเฟด

### what
Dragging a brake down a long descent heats it until it stops converting speed into heat as well as it did. On a small automatic with a drum rear, this is the failure mode of this road.

### story
The descents here are not short. Route 1095 drops off a ridge into the Pai valley over kilometres, not hundreds of metres, and the curve density means the brake is being used the whole way.

*Inference —* the rider who is in trouble is the one who found a speed that felt controlled at the top and held it by dragging. The brake gets hot, the lever travel grows, and because it grows gradually the rider compensates without noticing until there is no travel left. A drum brake filled with hot gas and glazed lining is the version of this that arrives fastest.

What prevents it is not stronger braking. It is **engine braking** and **stopping**. Down a gear (or, on an automatic, down to a speed the engine can hold), brake in firm short applications rather than a constant drag, and pull over every few kilometres on a long descent for two minutes. A brake that has faded comes back when it cools; one that has boiled its fluid may not.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-motorcycle-safety, s:mhs-measured

## Buses and pickups on your line (hazard/buses-on-your-line)
Thai: รถบัสและรถกระบะกินเลน

### what
Route 1095 and the mountain half of Route 108 are two lanes, and the minibuses, songthaews and delivery trucks that serve these towns take a hairpin by crossing the centre line.

### story
*Inference —* this is geometry, not bad driving. A vehicle with a long wheelbase physically cannot hold its own lane through a radius this tight, so it takes the width it needs. The rider's job is to assume it.

What that means on the road is that the correct position entering a blind left-hander is not the racing line. It is wide, slow enough to stop in the distance you can see, and off the centre line. The Chiang Mai to Pai minibus runs this road all day at a schedule, and it knows the corners far better than you do — which is the point: it is going faster than you through them and it is using your lane to do it.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-hairpin-turn, s:wp-motorcycle-safety

## Gravel on the apex (hazard/gravel-on-the-apex)
Thai: กรวดกลางโค้ง

### what
Sand, grit and washed gravel collect on the inside line of a hairpin and at the exit of a cutting. It is the most common surface hazard on this circuit and the least visible.

### story
*Inference —* the physical reason is simple: water running off a banked hillside crosses the road at the low point, which on a hairpin is the inside, and drops whatever it is carrying when it slows. So the loose material is not randomly distributed — it is where you were planning to put the front wheel.

The two places to expect it are the apex of an uphill hairpin and the first fifty metres after a cutting or a culvert. It is worst in the days after rain and after the rains end, when weeks of wash are still sitting there.

What to do about it is a line choice, not a skill: stay wide, turn late, get the bike upright before the throttle, and treat the inside third of a blind hairpin as though it is not there.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-motorcycle-safety, s:wp-hairpin-turn

## The low sun (hazard/low-sun)
Thai: แดดต่ำ

### what
Late afternoon on a westward leg in the cool season puts the sun directly down the road. A dusty visor turns it into a white sheet.

### story
*Inference —* the stretch this bites on is the westward run into Mae Hong Son, and it is one of the few arguments in the whole clockwise-versus-counter-clockwise question that has a physical cause rather than a preference behind it. Riding that leg in the morning puts the sun behind you.

The cheap fixes are a clean visor — a dusty one scatters light into a wall where a clean one does not — and simply stopping for twenty minutes, which on this circuit is never a hardship because there is always something to look at.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-motorcycle-safety

## Riding after dark (hazard/night-riding)
Thai: ขี่ตอนกลางคืน

### what
Once the sun is down the circuit has no ambient light at all outside the towns, and a rented bike's headlight is usually a single bulb of unknown age.

### story
*Inference —* three things stack. The headlight on a small rental is dim and often aimed badly. The hazards that matter here — gravel on the apex, a buffalo, a dog, a broken edge — are all low-contrast and low to the ground, which is exactly what a dipped beam shows worst. And the corner you cannot see round is a corner you cannot judge the radius of, on a road whose radii change constantly.

The practical rule people ride to is to be off the road by dusk and to plan legs so that arriving late is not required. Sunset in northern Thailand is early and quick year-round — this is near the tropics, so there is not much twilight to work with.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-motorcycle-safety, s:wp-geography-of-thailand

## Riding in the smoke (hazard/smoke-riding)
Thai: ขี่ในควัน

### what
In March and April the measured PM2.5 on this circuit sits above the US 24-hour standard on most days. On a bike you are breathing hard, at volume, for six hours.

### story
The visibility part is real and is worst at the viewpoints, which are the places that were the reason for stopping. A ridge that should show fifty kilometres shows two.

The breathing part is the one that matters. *Inference —* a rider at speed moves far more air through their lungs than someone walking, and an open-face helmet filters nothing at all. A fitted FFP2 or N95 worn under the helmet is what people use; a surgical mask, a buff or a bandana does not filter particles at this size. Anyone with asthma should treat March and April as a medical question and not a scheduling one.

There is also a third effect that gets missed: *Inference —* smoke flattens contrast, and flat contrast on a road whose whole difficulty is reading the next bend's radius is its own hazard. Slow down more than the visibility distance alone suggests.

Provenance: harvested · s:open-meteo-aq
Sources: s:open-meteo-aq, s:epa-pm25-2024, s:wp-southeast-asian-haze, s:wp-motorcycle-helmet

## The 700cc-and-up adventure bike (bike/big-adventure)
Thai: รถแอดเวนเจอร์ 700 ซีซีขึ้นไป

### what
An Africa Twin, a GS, a Tiger, a V-Strom 1050: 220 to 260 kilograms wet, tall, and entirely capable.

### story
**What it is like.** Commanding. You sit high enough to see over the vegetation into the next valley, the engine never has to try, and on the 265 kilometres of two-lane between Hot and Mae Hong Son it turns a long day into an easy one. Luggage is a solved problem. Nothing on this circuit is beyond it.

There is nothing on this circuit a large adventure bike cannot do. The question is arithmetic, not capability.

*Inference —* the measured curve density on Route 1095 and 1263 means a rider is making a steering input every few seconds for hours. On a light bike that is pleasure. At 250 kilograms it is work, and work accumulates: the mistakes on this road are made in the last hour of a long day, not the first.

The second arithmetic is the U-turn. A one-and-a-half-lane hairpin with a bank on one side and nothing on the other is a place where a tall, heavy bike has to be paddled round, and the surface there is often exactly the loose stuff that has washed down.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:wp-motorcycle-safety

## The 400–700 twin (bike/midweight-twin)
Thai: รถสองสูบ 400–700

### what
A CB500X, an MT-07, a Rally 500, a Himalayan 450: mid-capacity, torque low down, real brakes, and 17- or 19-inch wheels.

### story
**What it is like.** The sweet spot, if there is one. Enough torque to leave a hairpin without a downshift, brakes that never complain, and a seat you can stay on for six hours. On the long open sweeps of Route 108 south of Mae Sariang it is doing exactly what it was built for, and on 1095 it is still light enough to enjoy.

*Inference —* this is the range that suits the circuit best on paper: the engine braking to hold a descent, brakes that do not fade, enough power for the long Route 108 straights, and a weight you can still turn around on a one-and-a-half-lane switchback when you find a landslide.

The catch is the same weight. A 200-kilogram bike that falls over on a steep gravel guesthouse driveway needs two people to pick up, and on this circuit the second person may be an hour away.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-honda-500-twins
Sources: s:wp-honda-500-twins, s:wp-royal-enfield-himalayan

## Riding on the back (bike/on-the-back)
Thai: นั่งซ้อนท้าย

### what
Two people, one bike, six hundred kilometres of camber changes. Common, and worth planning around rather than discovering.

### story
**What it is like.** Better, in the ways nobody mentions. The passenger gets to look. The rider is working a line and watching the surface; the pillion is watching the valley open up, spotting the stall with the bench, seeing the gibbon. Two people on this road come home with different trips and the pillion's is often the richer one.

*Inference —* three things change with a passenger, and all three are worse on a descent. The bike is heavier so it stops later; the weight is high and behind the rear axle so it wants to stand the bike up mid-corner; and the passenger cannot see the road surface coming, so every unannounced brake application is a surprise that moves their weight forward into the rider.

What fixes most of it is boring: more distance, earlier braking, and telling the passenger where the next stop is. Days should be shorter — *Inference —* about two-thirds of the distance a solo rider would plan.

The pillion needs their own helmet, their own long sleeves and their own gloves, and the rental shop's spare helmet is often the one nobody chose.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:wp-motorcycle-safety, s:wp-motorcycle-helmet

## The 110–125 step-through (bike/step-through-110)
Thai: รถออโต้ 110–125 ซีซี

### what
A Honda Click, a Scoopy, a Mio, a Nouvo: automatic, small wheels, drum or single-disc brakes, and the rental shop's default. It will complete the loop. Several thousand a year do.

### story
**What it is like.** Feet forward, back straight, the whole valley in front of you because there is no screen and no tank. It weighs almost nothing, so you place it rather than steer it, and at forty kilometres an hour on a road this tight you are going quite fast enough to be busy. Everyone in northern Thailand is on one; you will be waved at by grandmothers.

Two things about a twist-and-go on a long mountain descent, and they are the same thing said twice.

An automatic transmission gives you **no engine braking worth the name**. On a road with the hairpin density of Route 1095 or 1263 that means the brakes do all the work for tens of kilometres at a stretch, and a small drum brake that has been dragged for four minutes stops working the way it did in the first minute. *Inference —* this is the single mechanical fact that most changes how a scooter should be ridden here: come down slowly, in stages, and stop to let the brakes cool, which feels absurd until the lever comes back to the bar.

Second, the wheels are small. A 12- or 14-inch wheel drops into a pothole a 17-inch wheel rides over, and the loop has potholes, gravel wash and edge break on every unsealed patch.

What it is good at is everything else: the towns, the fuel economy, the parking, the weight when you have dropped it, and the fact that any mechanic on the circuit has the parts.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-scooter-motorcycle
Sources: s:wp-scooter-motorcycle, s:wp-honda-click, s:wp-motorcycle-safety, s:mhs-measured

## The 250–450 trail bike (bike/trail-250)
Thai: รถวิบาก 250–450

### what
A KLX, a CRF, a D-Tracker, a Versys-X: long travel, 21- or 19-inch front wheel, upright, light, and rented all over Chiang Mai.

### story
**What it is like.** Tall, light and upright, which on a road with this many blind bends means you can see over the bank and around the corner before the corner arrives. The long suspension turns broken tarmac into texture rather than an event. It is the bike that makes every side road on the map a live option, and there are a great many side roads.

On a circuit that is sealed almost end to end, a trail bike's advantage is not the dirt. It is the suspension travel over broken edges, the ground clearance over the concrete water bars on steep sections, and the fact that dropping it at walking pace on a wet driveway costs nothing.

*Inference —* it is also the machine that makes Route 1263 and the side roads to the villages a decision you make on the day rather than one you make when you rent. What you give up is a comfortable 100 km/h on the four-lane section of Route 108 out of Chiang Mai, where a tall single-cylinder is buzzy and tiring.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-dual-sport-motorcycle
Sources: s:wp-dual-sport-motorcycle, s:mhs-measured

## The underbone with gears (bike/underbone-125)
Thai: รถครอบครัวมีเกียร์ 125

### what
A Honda Wave, a Dream, a Sonic: a small four-stroke in a step-through frame with a four-speed gearbox and usually a centrifugal clutch, so there are gears but no clutch lever. The machine most of northern Thailand actually rides.

### story
**What it is like.** The most satisfying cheap thing on two wheels. The clutchless gearbox means you change with your left foot and nothing else, so climbing becomes a rhythm — heel down, hold, heel down — and a long ascent stops being work. It is the bike the whole region actually rides, and riding one is the closest you get to travelling as a local rather than through a place.

The gearbox is the whole argument. Second gear holds a loaded 125 down a hairpin descent on the engine, and the brakes are then there for corners rather than for the entire hill. *Inference —* for a rider who has never come down ten kilometres of switchbacks before, this one change matters more than any amount of extra engine.

It is slower than a scooter off the line and faster everywhere that matters here, because 'faster' on this road means 'able to hold a steady speed up a long climb without the transmission hunting'.

The Super Cub layout it descends from has been in production since 1958 and is the most-produced motor vehicle in history, which is a way of saying that every mechanic between Chiang Mai and the Salween has seen one before.

Provenance: cited · s:wp-honda-super-cub
Sources: s:wp-honda-wave-series, s:wp-honda-super-cub, s:wp-underbone

## Sending a bag on the bus (kit/bus-parcel)
Thai: ฝากของไปกับรถโดยสาร

### what
Thai intercity and minibus operators carry parcels on the same departures that carry passengers. On this circuit that matters more than it does most places, because the bus is going exactly where you are going, on the same day.

### story
**Who runs the buses you would be using.** OpenStreetMap tags the operator at the Mae Malai stop and at the stop above Soppong as **Prempracha Transport**, and gives Pai's bus station the Thai name **เปรมประชาขนส่ง** — Prempracha Transport. That is the northern leg: Chiang Mai, Mae Malai, Pai, Soppong, Mae Hong Son, which is the clockwise route. Mae Hong Son, Khun Yuam and Mae Sariang all have their own bus stations on the southern leg. So a bag can be handed over at one end of a leg and collected at the other, on the run you are riding alongside.

**The step that makes it different from the post.** A posted parcel goes to an address, which means a guesthouse has to agree in advance to receive a bag for a guest who has not arrived. A bus parcel goes to **the operator's counter at the destination bus station**, and you collect it yourself when you get to town. Nobody else has to agree to anything. *Inference —* on a route where you are arriving in a different town every evening, that is the simpler arrangement by a distance.
